```{python}
import altair as alt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import beta as beta_dist
from src.plotting import apply_lex_altair_theme

apply_lex_altair_theme()
alt.data_transformers.disable_max_rows()

n_steps = 50
fixed_beta = 10
p_grid = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 300)

rows = []
for step in range(n_steps + 1):
    alpha = 2 + step
    beta = fixed_beta
    density = beta_dist.pdf(p_grid, alpha, beta)

    rows.extend(
        {
            "p": p,
            "density": d,
            "step": step,
        }
        for p, d in zip(p_grid, density)
    )

beta_updates = pd.DataFrame(rows)
final_update = beta_updates[beta_updates["step"] == n_steps]

lines = alt.Chart(beta_updates[beta_updates["step"] < n_steps]).mark_line(
    color="#ddb06d",
    strokeWidth=1.0,
).encode(
    x=alt.X("p:Q", axis=None, scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 1])),
    y=alt.Y("density:Q", axis=None),
    detail="step:N",
    opacity=alt.Opacity(
        "step:Q",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, n_steps], range=[0.05, 0.95]),
        legend=None,
    ),
)

final_line = alt.Chart(final_update).mark_line(
    color="#ddb06d",
    strokeWidth=3.0,
).encode(
    x=alt.X("p:Q", axis=None, scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 1])),
    y=alt.Y("density:Q", axis=None),
)

(lines + final_line).properties(
    width="container",
    height=250,
).configure_view(
    stroke=None,
)
```

# My introduction to Bayes

I now consider myself a software engineer, but my journey into programming started with
an interest in probability and uncertainty.

In the early days I was doing little experiments in spreadsheets, bumping around in a
dark room without much ability to navigate. Around the same time I also started getting
exposed to blogs like [Less Wrong](https://www.lesswrong.com/) and the writings of
Eliezer Yudkowsky---who, incidentally, is currently sounding the alarm that
superintelligent AI is going to [literally kill everyone if we build
it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_Anyone_Builds_It,_Everyone_Dies)---but this post
isn't about existential dread, or the unmooring mental effect of having one of your
foremost intellectual influences prophesying imminent doom.

Less Wrong and Eliezer introduced me properly to Bayes. I say properly, because reading
a Wikipedia article or having professors gleefully show how "unintuitive" it is, is
about the _worst_ way you could possibly be introduced to it. These writings were not
gleeful in challenging intuition, but patient and aphoristic, teaching by example
through excellent technical writings, rather than whiteboard problems. 

Bayes intersected with my work, and my interest in uncertainty, so these influences came
together at a great time in my career. 

More importantly, the introduction to Bayes was a formalized introduction to rationality
and probabilistic thinking in general, which for whatever reason I am very predisposed
to, and following that rabbit hole led me to Bayesian statistics. 

This led me to dig for more influences, like [E.T
Jaynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Thompson_Jaynes), [Aubrey
Clayton](https://aubreyclayton.com/), Cameron Davidson-Pilon's [Bayesian Methods for
Hackers](https://github.com/camdavidsonpilon/probabilistic-programming-and-bayesian-methods-for-hackers)
and the incredible work (in lectures and textbooks) of [Richard
McElreath](https://www.routledge.com/Statistical-Rethinking-A-Bayesian-Course-with-Examples-in-R-and-STAN/McElreath/p/book/9780367139919).

Bayesian statistics required me to program, so I learned, and on the way learned that my
home was always going to be in software engineering, I just hadn't landed on that path
yet. So Bayesian statistics, in the end, is the reason I am doing what I'm doing today.

And software engineering combined with Bayesian statistics is a very powerful
combination, as it turns out.

Because I'm not a formally trained statistician (or an academic of any kind), but
instead someone who works in a technical industry where engineering and data analytics
are highly valued, my perspective on where Bayes fits in is as much value-oriented as it
is driven by intellectual curiosity. I've written before about the idea of
[informatics](https://nick-dorsch.github.io/blog/posts/informatics/), and Bayesian
statistics sits at the heart of the concept.

The point I want to make in this post boils down to this: the Bayesian toolkit lets us
combine domain knowledge and limited data into highly expressive, interpretable models
that quantify uncertainty, and this makes them ideal for decision support in complex
technical domains.

# The core of it

> A. _"What should we believe, given our understanding of the world and our data?"_
>
> B. _"What should we do, given that information?"_

Bayes helps us define what to believe, decision theory formalizes what actions to take,
and our values ultimately decide what we do.

In contexts where decisions are difficult, uncertainty is an essential ingredient. You
really can't make good decisions in the absence of a consideration of uncertainty---we
do it all the time by calling options "safe bets" or "high-risk"---probability models
just quantify these considerations and make them explicit. 

The uncertainty is ultimately subjective (all probabilities are in the Bayesian view),
but subjective quantities still follow rules. If you want to follow your uncertainties
through to their logical consequences, you need to follow them.

# Monte Carlo models

Monte Carlo models are the first thing to master when learning how to use probability.
They are incredibly flexible and simple in concept. Define your uncertainties, state
the math that governs the outputs you care about, and run the system thousands of times
to see what happens.

You can teach yourself a lot by doing this. You will discover
[SEM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_error) by adding stochastic outputs
together. You will quickly disabuse yourself of mental mistakes relating to "stacking
percentiles" because you can watch the real result occur in simulation. You will
understand CDFs and PDFs and quantile ranges without even knowing their names, because
you will understand that behind everything is an array of simulated values, not a
mysterious system of mathematics that is beyond your understanding.

You can start doing this without even understanding the probability distributions in the
background---that understanding will come as you delve deeper.

## Back of the envelope thinking

In [The Art of Doing Science and
Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Art_of_Doing_Science_and_Engineering) by
Richard Hamming, he talks about the usefulness of back of the envelope problem solving.
Modern computing gives us the tools to take back of the envelope problem solving into
the probabilistic realm with minimal effort.

One of Hamming's examples is the idea that (back when he wrote the book in the late
80s) 90% of the scientists who have ever lived are now alive. He takes that statement
along with an assumption that knowledge doubles every 17 years, to do a back of the
envelope calculation to see how compatible the two statements are.

I will skip the maths (apparently integral calculus was part of Hamming's idea of back
of the envelope thinking), but he shows that if the number of scientists practicing at
any time is given by:

$$
y(t) = ae^{bt}
$$

and, assuming scientists have careers lasting around 55 years, the proportion alive
today is given by:

$$
1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{55/17} = 0.894...
$$

And he makes the point well. Comfort with turning claims into a bit of maths allows him
to test assumptions with minimal effort, and in this case he is left satisfied that the
claims are consistent.

Modern computing and tooling means that for us, with a laptop and a Python install, we
can add our uncertainty to the mix with minimal effort. Say we think the doubling time
is centred on 17 years, and the length of a scientist's career is centred on 55 years,
but we're uncertain about both quantities:

```python
import numpy as np

n = 5_000

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
career_years = rng.normal(55, 10, n)
doubling_years = rng.normal(17, 3, n)

proportion_alive = 1 - (1 / 2) ** (career_years / doubling_years)
```

```{python}
import altair as alt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from src.plotting import apply_lex_altair_theme

apply_lex_altair_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 5_000

career_years = rng.normal(55, 10, n)
doubling_years = rng.normal(17, 3, n)

proportion_alive = 1 - (1 / 2) ** (career_years / doubling_years)
results = pd.DataFrame({"proportion_alive": proportion_alive})

mean_result = results["proportion_alive"].mean()
low, high = results["proportion_alive"].quantile([0.05, 0.95])
print(f"Mean result: {mean_result:.3f}; 90% interval: {low:.3f}–{high:.3f}")

hist = (
    alt.Chart(results)
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "proportion_alive:Q",
            bin=alt.Bin(maxbins=80),
            title="Proportion of all scientists alive today",
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        y=alt.Y(
            "count():Q",
            axis=alt.Axis(labels=False, ticks=False, title=None, grid=False),
        ),
        tooltip=["count()"],
    )
    .properties(width="container")
)

mean_rule = (
    alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({"x": [mean_result]}))
    .mark_rule(color="red")
    .encode(x="x:Q")
)

hist + mean_rule
```

Maybe we care about this uncertainty, maybe we don't, it depends on the problem and the
stakes. The point is that it is _incredibly easy to do_, and now with AI, all that is
stopping you is a passing familiarity with the concepts, and just asking!

## Scale to any problem

Monte Carlo models can be self-contained and simple, like the above example, or they can
get [arbitrarily complex](https://nick-dorsch.github.io/blog/posts/resgo/), but the
_style of thinking_ that makes it clear how this trick is done is all you need to start.
You will pick up more complex concepts like multivariate correlated sampling, working
with high dimensional arrays, and vectorization as you delve deeper, but the core
framework is incredibly simple to start with. 

Just make the computer go _brrrrrr_.

# Learning from Data

It might appear that I've diverged from the point of this post (using Bayes to solve
technical problems and improve decision making) but the Monte Carlo method begs a
question:

How do we decide what distributions to use? And how do we parametrize them?

Formalizing uncertainty in a Monte Carlo model is great, but how can we be rigorous
about the parameters that define the distributions that model that uncertainty?

In the example above I set the year length of a scientist's career to $\text{Normal}(55,
10)$... but I just pulled that distribution out of a hat.

In Bayesian statistics terms this would be called _elicitation_. We ask someone what
they think is a reasonable range of values for a particular quantity (before looking at
any data) and we take their answer and "elicit" an appropriate distribution that
captures that belief.

But there is no data here, how do we take that _prior_ belief about the quantity and use
data to learn about it?

That requires Bayes.

$$
p(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(y)}
$$

The left side of that equation means, in words, _What is the posterior probability
distribution over the model parameters, given the observed data_, which sounds similar
to 

> A. _"What should we believe, given our understanding of the world and our data?"_

In technical contexts these are the same thing, because our beliefs are formalized by
the parameters in our Monte Carlo models.

So now we've added data ($y$), how do we use it in practice?

The field of Bayesian statistics is devoted to this problem.

## Markov Chain Monte Carlo models

It turns out that Bayes theorem is a huge pain in the ass. There are classes of problem
where the maths solves [elegantly](https://nick-dorsch.github.io/blog/posts/lindy/),
providing efficient analytical solutions to Bayesian models. These are very cool and
useful to learn, but also rare when applied to real-world problems.

Most of the time, we need specialized algorithms to do Bayes. It is all because of this
innocent looking probability in the denominator of Bayes theorem:

$$
p(y)
$$

Which equates to

$$
p(y) = \int p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)\,d\theta
$$

> _"The denominator is the probability of the observed data under the whole model. It
> integrates over every possible value of $\theta$, weighting each value by its prior
> plausibility. In other words, it asks how surprising the data would be before we knew
> which parameter value was true."_

That sentence is a headache. I actually asked the AI to write it because I couldn't
manage a sentence describing it.

It turns out it is a headache for computers, too, because most of the time that integral
is an intractable nightmare, where no analytical solution even exists.

Instead, clever algorithms are needed to approximate the posterior distribution through
random sampling. This is Monte Carlo again, but this time we have no inverse CDF to use
(the function used to generate random samples in Monte Carlo models) as the posterior
distribution is unknown, so we have to explore the probability space without it,
somehow. That is where Markov Chain Monte Carlo
([MCMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)) algorithms come in.

Learning how to build efficient models to do Bayesian inference is the engineering side
of Bayesian statistics.

This isn't a post about that engineering effort, but the point is, with MCMC models,
we can update our beliefs with data across a wide range of problems.

## What about Machine Learning and AI?

The dominant paradigm in data science is machine learning. Many mainstream machine
learning workflows are built around optimization: choose a model class, define a loss
function, and find the parameters that make the best in-sample predictions while
minimizing out-of-sample error. For big datasets with many features, this can work
incredibly well.

But running problems through the black box of ML costs us a few important things.

First is expressiveness. Engineering problems usually have an underlying mathematical
structure that is well understood. It is not wise to throw it out and expect the
algorithm to pick it all up again using large quantities of data. Physics informed
neural networks
([PINNs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics-informed_neural_networks)) address this
problem, embedding physical laws into neural network training such that solutions are
kept within physically consistent constraints, but they are not the norm in the ML
world---most of the time ML models are not constrained in this way.

Second is uncertainty. Most machine learning algorithsm do not provide uncertainty
quantification. Especially in complex domains with limited data, that uncertainty can be
an essential component of effective decision making. In high stakes situations, an ML
model stating that the answer is "25!" while not having any ability to provide
confidence intervals of $\pm 10$ or $\pm 1000$ makes decision making based on their
results far less robust.

Third is what I call the problem of "small data". Big data is a luxury that most
engineering problems don't enjoy. Instead we are often trying to maximize the
information we can get out of small quantities of expensive to acquired data. Machine
learning solutions in this context are not the best choice, in my view. They will
provide uninterpretable solutions with questionable validity, with no uncertainty
preservation.

Machine learning is a rich field with many answers to the issues I bring up here, but my
answer is: use Bayes instead. I just think it is a better toolset in many engineering
contexts.

# Examples

I want to show a few examples here. My background is in oil and gas, so that is where I
know problems in the most detail, but I want to stress how domain agnostic Bayesian
statistics is. If you have a system of equations that govern behaviour in some domain
you are studying, you can express it in a Bayesian model, feed it data, and do
inference.

These models are created and run with [PyMC](https://www.pymc.io/welcome.html), a
popular Python package for doing Bayesian statistics.

## Oil Field Volumetrics

A classic petroleum engineering example is a volumetric estimate. The deterministic
calculation is simple, but every input is uncertain: porosity, water saturation, net to
gross, gross rock volume, and the oil formation volume factor. Offset wells can teach us
about reservoir properties, while others properties are derived from separate studies,
like geophysics driven structural modelling, or PVT driven formation volume factor
calculations.

Here is a small PyMC model using synthetic offset-well data. The 25 wells inform field
average porosity, water saturation, and net-to-gross. The formation volume factor, $B_o$, and
gross rock volume, GRV, are included as priors with no direct observations. STOIIP is then
calculated as a deterministic variable from the posterior mean reservoir parameters.

Here is a sample of the (synthetic) data:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n_wells = 25

# Synthetic offset-well data: porosity, Sw, and net-to-gross as fractions.
offset_wells = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "well": [f"W-{i:02d}" for i in range(1, n_wells + 1)],
        "porosity": np.clip(rng.normal(0.21, 0.025, n_wells), 0.12, 0.32),
        "sw": np.clip(rng.normal(0.33, 0.04, n_wells), 0.15, 0.60),
        "net_to_gross": np.clip(rng.normal(0.42, 0.07, n_wells), 0.15, 0.80),
    }
)

offset_wells.head()
```

```{python}
#| output: false
import pymc as pm

with pm.Model() as volumetrics_model:
    # Field-level reservoir property means learned from offset wells.
    phi_mu = pm.Beta("phi_mu", alpha=2, beta=8)      # prior mean = 0.20
    sw_mu = pm.Beta("sw_mu", alpha=3, beta=7)        # prior mean = 0.30
    ntg_mu = pm.Beta("ntg_mu", alpha=4, beta=6)      # prior mean = 0.40

    # Offset-well likelihoods.
    pm.Normal(
        "porosity_obs",
        mu=phi_mu,
        sigma=0.025,
        observed=offset_wells["porosity"].to_numpy(),
    )
    pm.Normal(
        "sw_obs",
        mu=sw_mu,
        sigma=0.04,
        observed=offset_wells["sw"].to_numpy(),
    )
    pm.Normal(
        "net_to_gross_obs",
        mu=ntg_mu,
        sigma=0.07,
        observed=offset_wells["net_to_gross"].to_numpy(),
    )

    # Prior-only quantities: no direct data yet.
    bo = pm.LogNormal("bo", mu=np.log(1.25), sigma=0.05)          # reservoir bbl / STB
    grv = pm.LogNormal("grv_acft", mu=np.log(18_000), sigma=0.1) # gross rock volume, acre-ft

    # Stock tank oil initially in place. 7,758 converts acre-ft of pore volume to barrels.
    stoiip_stb = pm.Deterministic(
        "stoiip_stb",
        7_758 * grv * ntg_mu * phi_mu * (1 - sw_mu) / bo,
    )
    stoiip_mmbbl = pm.Deterministic("stoiip_mmbbl", stoiip_stb / 1_000_000)

    prior = pm.sample_prior_predictive(
        draws=8000,
        var_names=["stoiip_mmbbl"],
        random_seed=42,
    )

    trace = pm.sample(
        draws=2_000,
        tune=1_000,
        chains=4,
        target_accept=0.9,
        random_seed=42,
    )
```

Here is a graph representation of the statistical model, grey nodes indicate observations:

```{python}
pm.model_to_graphviz(volumetrics_model)
```

And here is the result:

```{python}
import altair as alt

prior_stoiip = prior.prior["stoiip_mmbbl"].values.ravel()
posterior_stoiip = trace.posterior["stoiip_mmbbl"].values.ravel()

# Use common bins so the prior and posterior histograms are directly comparable.
upper = np.quantile(np.concatenate([prior_stoiip, posterior_stoiip]), 0.995)
bins = np.linspace(0, upper, 60)


def make_histogram(samples, label):
    density, edges = np.histogram(samples, bins=bins, density=True)
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "stoiip_mmbbl": edges[:-1],
            "density": density,
            "distribution": label,
        }
    )


prior_hist = make_histogram(prior_stoiip, "Prior")
posterior_hist = make_histogram(posterior_stoiip, "Posterior")

color = alt.Color(
    "distribution:N",
    scale=alt.Scale(domain=["Prior", "Posterior"], range=["#5b6770", "#ddb06d"]),
    legend=alt.Legend(
        title=None,
        orient="none",
        legendX=520,
        legendY=10,
        direction="vertical",
    ),
)

posterior_area = (
    alt.Chart(posterior_hist)
    .mark_area(
        interpolate="step-after",
        opacity=0.45,
        line={"strokeWidth": 2},
    )
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "stoiip_mmbbl:Q",
            title="STOIIP, MMSTB",
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        y=alt.Y(
            "density:Q",
            title=None,
            axis=alt.Axis(labels=False, ticks=False, grid=False),
        ),
        color=color,
    )
)

prior_line = (
    alt.Chart(prior_hist)
    .mark_line(
        interpolate="step-after",
        strokeWidth=2,
    )
    .encode(
        x="stoiip_mmbbl:Q",
        y="density:Q",
        color=color,
    )
)

(posterior_area + prior_line).properties(width="container", height=320)
```

Here I'm showing the prior STOIIP (the distribution that the subsurface team might have
estimated before discovering this field), and the well data driven posterior STOIIP,
which has converged on a tighter uncertainty around the true value as average field
reservoir properties are sampled.

The point of putting the volumetric equation inside the probabilistic model is that the
STOIIP output is not a separate spreadsheet calculation bolted on afterwards. It
is part of the model graph. The same samples that update porosity, water saturation, and
net pay from the offset wells also propagate the prior uncertainty in GRV and $B_o$ into
the final volume estimate.

Making the STOIIP part of the model graph also makes some advanced modelling possible,
like integrating observed production as an additional constraint. If 4 MMSTB had already
been recovered from this reservoir, for example, it would indicate STOIIP values less
than ~8 MMSTB are highly unlikely, as recoveries of greater than 50% in oil reservoirs
are uncommon.

## Fluid contact uncertainty from RFT data

Another fun example in the oil and gas context is estimating fluid contacts based on
pressure points taken in reservoirs. One can infer the depth of a gas-water contact
based on this data, but it is often an uncertain estimate due to unknown fluid
properties like the salinity of the brine (water) and the density of the gas. The water
gradient is also often far less well sampled than gas columns.

The problem boils down to finding the intersection of two lines: the gas pressure
gradient and the water pressure gradient. The intersection of two lines is computable
as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= m_1 x + b_1 \\
y_2 &= m_2 x + b_2 \\
 x^* &= \frac{b_2 - b_1}{m_1 - m_2} \\
 y^* &= m_1 x^* + b_1
      = \frac{m_1 b_2 - m_2 b_1}{m_1 - m_2}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we can model those pressure gradients with a Bayesian statistical model, we will also
get full uncertainty quantification for the pressure and (of more interest) the depth of
the intersection, which represents the gas-water contact.

Let's start by simulating some data:

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

gwc_depth_mss = -1500.0
gas_column_height_m = 100.0
contact_pressure_mpa = 20.0
water_gradient_mpa_per_m = 0.0102
gas_gradient_mpa_per_m = 0.0022
gas_pressure_error_mpa = 0.005
water_pressure_error_mpa = 0.1

# Subsea depth is negative down. The gas column extends from -1400 to -1500 mSS,
# and the water points are sparse below the contact.
gas_depth_mss = np.linspace(
    gwc_depth_mss + gas_column_height_m,
    gwc_depth_mss + 50,
    5,
)
water_depth_mss = np.array([-1380, -1520, -1530, -1585, -1630])

# Pressure increases downwards. Since depth is negative down, the vertical distance
# below the contact is gwc_depth_mss - depth_mss.
gas_pressure_mpa = (
    contact_pressure_mpa
    + gas_gradient_mpa_per_m * (gwc_depth_mss - gas_depth_mss)
    + rng.normal(0, gas_pressure_error_mpa, gas_depth_mss.size)
)
water_pressure_mpa = (
    contact_pressure_mpa
    + water_gradient_mpa_per_m * (gwc_depth_mss - water_depth_mss)
    + rng.normal(0, water_pressure_error_mpa, water_depth_mss.size)
)

rft_data = pd.concat(
    [
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "fluid": "Gas",
                "depth_mss": gas_depth_mss,
                "pressure_mpa": gas_pressure_mpa,
            }
        ),
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "fluid": "Water",
                "depth_mss": water_depth_mss,
                "pressure_mpa": water_pressure_mpa,
            }
        ),
    ],
    ignore_index=True,
)
```

```{python}
rft_points = (
    alt.Chart(rft_data)
    .mark_circle(size=80, opacity=0.85)
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "pressure_mpa:Q",
            title="Pressure, MPa",
            scale=alt.Scale(zero=False),
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        y=alt.Y(
            "depth_mss:Q",
            title="Depth, mSS",
            scale=alt.Scale(zero=False),
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        color=alt.Color(
            "fluid:N",
            scale=alt.Scale(
                domain=["Water", "Gas"],
                range=["#9bd3e6", "#f4a6a6"],
            ),
            legend=alt.Legend(title=None),
        ),
        tooltip=["fluid", "depth_mss", "pressure_mpa"],
    )
    .properties(width="container", height=360)
)

rft_points
```

Each pressure gradient is a linear function, so our Bayesian model is simply estimating
the slope and intercept of each, and then passing the solution for the intersection of
them into the model graph, to output it as an uncertain parameter.

```{python}
#| output: false

water_data = rft_data[rft_data["fluid"] == "Water"]
gas_data = rft_data[rft_data["fluid"] == "Gas"]

# Centering depth around the expected contact keeps the intercept priors intuitive:
# they represent pressure near the contact depth.
depth_ref_mss = -1500.0
water_depth_centered = water_data["depth_mss"].to_numpy() - depth_ref_mss
gas_depth_centered = gas_data["depth_mss"].to_numpy() - depth_ref_mss

with pm.Model() as contact_model:
    water_intercept = pm.Normal("water_intercept", mu=20.0, sigma=1.0)
    gas_intercept = pm.Normal("gas_intercept", mu=20.0, sigma=1.0)

    water_slope = pm.Normal("water_slope", mu=-0.010, sigma=0.002)
    gas_slope = pm.Normal("gas_slope", mu=-0.002, sigma=0.001)

    water_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("water_sigma", sigma=0.15)
    gas_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("gas_sigma", sigma=0.15)

    water_pressure_mu = pm.Deterministic(
        "water_pressure_mu",
        water_intercept + water_slope * water_depth_centered,
    )
    gas_pressure_mu = pm.Deterministic(
        "gas_pressure_mu",
        gas_intercept + gas_slope * gas_depth_centered,
    )

    pm.Normal(
        "water_pressure_obs",
        mu=water_pressure_mu,
        sigma=water_sigma,
        observed=water_data["pressure_mpa"].to_numpy(),
    )
    pm.Normal(
        "gas_pressure_obs",
        mu=gas_pressure_mu,
        sigma=gas_sigma,
        observed=gas_data["pressure_mpa"].to_numpy(),
    )

    contact_depth_mss = pm.Deterministic(
        "contact_depth_mss",
        depth_ref_mss + (gas_intercept - water_intercept) / (water_slope - gas_slope),
    )

    contact_trace = pm.sample(
        draws=2_000,
        tune=1_000,
        chains=4,
        target_accept=0.9,
        random_seed=42,
    )
```

```{python}
pm.model_to_graphviz(contact_model)
```

Fitting the model to the data yields our two pressure gradients:

```{python}
def posterior_gradient_interval(trace, fluid, depth_grid_mss):
    intercept = trace.posterior[f"{fluid}_intercept"].values.ravel()
    slope = trace.posterior[f"{fluid}_slope"].values.ravel()
    depth_centered = depth_grid_mss - depth_ref_mss

    pressure = intercept[:, None] + slope[:, None] * depth_centered[None, :]
    pressure_low, pressure_mid, pressure_high = np.quantile(
        pressure,
        [0.025, 0.5, 0.975],
        axis=0,
    )

    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "fluid": fluid.title(),
            "depth_mss": depth_grid_mss,
            "pressure_low": pressure_low,
            "pressure_mid": pressure_mid,
            "pressure_high": pressure_high,
        }
    )


depth_grid = np.linspace(
    water_data["depth_mss"].min() - 10,
    water_data["depth_mss"].max(),
    100,
)

gradient_intervals = pd.concat(
    [
        posterior_gradient_interval(contact_trace, "water", depth_grid),
        posterior_gradient_interval(contact_trace, "gas", depth_grid),
    ],
    ignore_index=True,
)

fluid_color = alt.Color(
    "fluid:N",
    scale=alt.Scale(
        domain=["Water", "Gas"],
        range=["#9bd3e6", "#f4a6a6"],
    ),
    legend=alt.Legend(title=None),
)

interval_band = (
    alt.Chart(gradient_intervals)
    .mark_area(opacity=0.25)
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "pressure_low:Q",
            title="Pressure, MPa",
            scale=alt.Scale(zero=False),
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        x2="pressure_high:Q",
        y=alt.Y(
            "depth_mss:Q",
            title="Depth, mSS",
            scale=alt.Scale(zero=False),
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        color=fluid_color,
    )
)

median_gradient = (
    alt.Chart(gradient_intervals)
    .mark_line(strokeWidth=2)
    .encode(
        x="pressure_mid:Q",
        y="depth_mss:Q",
        color=fluid_color,
    )
)

rft_points = (
    alt.Chart(rft_data)
    .mark_circle(size=80, opacity=0.85)
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "pressure_mpa:Q",
            title="Pressure, MPa",
            scale=alt.Scale(zero=False),
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        y=alt.Y(
            "depth_mss:Q",
            title="Depth, mSS",
            scale=alt.Scale(zero=False),
            axis=alt.Axis(grid=False),
        ),
        color=fluid_color,
        tooltip=["fluid", "depth_mss", "pressure_mpa"],
    )
)

(interval_band + median_gradient + rft_points).properties(width="container", height=360)
```

And the uncertain intersection of those two lines is the uncertainty in the contact
depth, also shown below as a histogram:

```{python}
contact_depth_hist, contact_depth_edges = np.histogram(

contact_depth_df = pd.DataFrame(
```

Neat!

## Fluid compositional modelling

A Dirichlet model can be fit to a dataset of fluid samples to model uncertainty in
composition across a field. This example benefits from hierarchical modelling (a
Bayesian statistical superpower) to account for groupings of data, like replicate
samples of the same interval, or samples from the same reservoir.

Again, we start with some synthetic data:

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

components = ["C1", "C2", "C3", "C4", "C5", "C6", "C7+"]

reservoir_profiles = {
    "Reservoir A": np.array([0.72, 0.10, 0.06, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.03]),
    "Reservoir B": np.array([0.34, 0.11, 0.10, 0.26, 0.06, 0.04, 0.09]),
    "Reservoir C": np.array([0.24, 0.10, 0.09, 0.08, 0.08, 0.07, 0.34]),
}

reservoir_concentration = {
    "Reservoir A": 120,
    "Reservoir B": 80,
    "Reservoir C": 60,
}

base_samples_per_reservoir = 8
replicate_concentration = 1_500
replicate_probabilities = [0.65, 0.25, 0.10]
replicate_counts = [1, 2, 3]

rows = []
for reservoir, profile in reservoir_profiles.items():
    reservoir_alpha = profile * reservoir_concentration[reservoir]

    for sample_idx in range(1, base_samples_per_reservoir + 1):
        sample_group = f"{reservoir[-1]}-{sample_idx:02d}"
        base_composition = rng.dirichlet(reservoir_alpha)
        n_replicates = rng.choice(replicate_counts, p=replicate_probabilities)

        for replicate_idx in range(1, n_replicates + 1):
            observed_composition = rng.dirichlet(
                base_composition * replicate_concentration
            )

            rows.append(
                {
                    "sample_id": f"{sample_group}-{replicate_idx}",
                    "sample_group": sample_group,
                    "replicate": replicate_idx,
                    "reservoir": reservoir,
                    **dict(zip(components, observed_composition)),
                }
            )

composition_samples = pd.DataFrame(rows)

composition_samples_long = composition_samples.melt(
    id_vars=["sample_id", "sample_group", "replicate", "reservoir"],
    value_vars=components,
    var_name="component",
    value_name="fraction",
)
```

```{python}
mean_composition = (
    composition_samples_long
    .groupby(["reservoir", "component"], as_index=False)
    .agg(mean_fraction=("fraction", "mean"))
)

alt.Chart(mean_composition).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X(
        "component:N",
        title="Component",
        sort=components,
        axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0, grid=False),
    ),
    xOffset=alt.XOffset("reservoir:N", title="Reservoir"),
    y=alt.Y(
        "mean_fraction:Q",
        title="Mean mole fraction",
        axis=alt.Axis(format="%", grid=False),
    ),
    color=alt.Color("reservoir:N", title="Reservoir"),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("reservoir:N", title="Reservoir"),
        alt.Tooltip("component:N", title="Component"),
        alt.Tooltip("mean_fraction:Q", title="Mean fraction", format=".1%"),
    ],
).properties(
    width="container",
    height=320,
)
```

Note these are the _average_ compositions of the three reservoirs, in reality we have
several fluid samples (and replicates) in a dataset of 238 total samples.

So how can we model the average properties by reservoir, and the variability we see
within sample intervals and across them?

```{python}
#| output: false
composition_observed = composition_samples[components].to_numpy()

reservoir_codes, reservoir_names = pd.factorize(composition_samples["reservoir"])
group_codes, group_names = pd.factorize(composition_samples["sample_group"])

group_lookup = (
    composition_samples[["sample_group", "reservoir"]]
    .drop_duplicates()
    .set_index("sample_group")
    .loc[group_names]
)
group_reservoir_codes = pd.Categorical(
    group_lookup["reservoir"], categories=reservoir_names
).codes

coords = {
    "component": components,
    "reservoir": reservoir_names,
    "sample_group": group_names,
    "sample": composition_samples["sample_id"],
}

with pm.Model(coords=coords) as composition_model:
    reservoir_pooling = pm.Exponential("reservoir_pooling", lam=1 / 20)
    group_pooling = pm.Exponential("group_pooling", lam=1 / 100)

    global_alpha = pm.Gamma(
        "global_alpha",
        alpha=2,
        beta=0.2,
        dims="component",
    )

    reservoir_alpha = pm.Gamma(
        "reservoir_alpha",
        alpha=global_alpha[None, :] * reservoir_pooling,
        beta=reservoir_pooling,
        dims=("reservoir", "component"),
    )

    group_alpha = pm.Gamma(
        "group_alpha",
        alpha=reservoir_alpha[group_reservoir_codes] * group_pooling,
        beta=group_pooling,
        dims=("sample_group", "component"),
    )

    pm.Dirichlet(
        "composition",
        a=group_alpha[group_codes],
        observed=composition_observed,
        dims=("sample", "component"),
    )

    composition_trace = pm.sample(
        draws=2_000,
        tune=1_000,
        chains=4,
        target_accept=0.9,
        random_seed=42,
    )
```

```{python}
pm.model_to_graphviz(composition_model)
```

```{python}
#| output: false
histogram_bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 250)
histogram_rows = []

for reservoir in reservoir_names:
    reservoir_alpha = (
        composition_trace.posterior["reservoir_alpha"]
        .sel(reservoir=reservoir)
        .values
    )
    reservoir_alpha = reservoir_alpha.reshape(-1, len(components))
    reservoir_composition = reservoir_alpha / reservoir_alpha.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

    for component_idx, component in enumerate(components):
        density, edges = np.histogram(
            reservoir_composition[:, component_idx],
            bins=histogram_bins,
            density=True,
        )
        histogram_rows.extend(
            {
                "reservoir": reservoir,
                "component": component,
                "fraction": edges[i],
                "density": density[i],
                "component_order": component_idx,
            }
            for i in range(len(density))
        )

reservoir_composition_hist = pd.DataFrame(histogram_rows)

component_color = alt.Color(
    "component:N",
    sort=components,
    scale=alt.Scale(
        domain=components,
        range=["#ddb06d", "#9bd3e6", "#f4a6a6", "#8fbc8f", "#b58fd3", "#f0c987", "#5b6770"],
    ),
    legend=alt.Legend(title=None),
)


def reservoir_composition_histogram(reservoir):
    reservoir_hist = reservoir_composition_hist[
        reservoir_composition_hist["reservoir"] == reservoir
    ]

    return alt.Chart(reservoir_hist).mark_line(
        interpolate="step-after",
        strokeWidth=2,
    ).encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "fraction:Q",
            title="Posterior mole fraction",
            scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 1]),
            axis=alt.Axis(format="%", grid=False),
        ),
        y=alt.Y(
            "density:Q",
            title=None,
            axis=alt.Axis(labels=False, ticks=False, grid=False),
        ),
        color=component_color,
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("reservoir:N", title="Reservoir"),
            alt.Tooltip("component:N", title="Component"),
            alt.Tooltip("fraction:Q", title="Posterior fraction", format=".1%"),
            alt.Tooltip("density:Q", title="Density", format=".2f"),
        ],
    ).properties(
        title=reservoir,
        width="container",
        height=260,
    )
```

```{python}
reservoir_composition_histogram("Reservoir A")
```

